youtube.baslik: Intraoperative Monitoring: Hearing and Facial Nerve | Lesson 203 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How are hearing and the facial nerve protected during surgery? In this lesson we cover hearing monitoring with ABR, ECochG and direct nerve recording in cerebellopontine angle surgery, free-running and triggered EMG for the facial nerve, the effect of anesthesia, and the audiologist's role in the operating room team.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Hall, New Handbook of Auditory Evoked Responses; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology; Møller, Intraoperative Neurophysiological Monitoring; Romstöck et al., Continuous electromyography monitoring of motor cranial nerves during cerebellopontine angle surgery, Journal of Neurosurgery (2000); ASHA, Neurophysiologic Intraoperative Monitoring (1992); AAO-HNS, Position Statement: Intraoperative Nerve Monitoring in Otologic Surgery.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: Monitoring hearing and the facial nerve in surgery
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how evoked potentials are used in the operating room to protect nerves.
We will cover hearing monitoring in cerebellopontine angle surgery, facial nerve electromyography and the audiologist's role in the team.
In the vestibular schwannoma lesson, we saw that four nerves travel together in the internal auditory canal.
The superior and inferior vestibular nerves lie in the posterior part; the tumor usually arises from these nerves.
The cochlear nerve runs in the anterior inferior part, and the facial nerve in the anterior superior part.
The labyrinthine artery, which supplies these nerves and the inner ear, passes through the same narrow canal.
While the tumor is removed, these structures can be stretched, heated or lose their blood supply.
Intraoperative monitoring means tracking the function of these nerves in real time throughout the operation.
The aim is to detect stress on a nerve before permanent damage occurs and to tell the surgeon.
On receiving a warning, the surgeon can reduce traction, change the working area or pause briefly.
Monitoring leaves decisions to the surgeon; it only gives timely and reliable information.
According to ENT position statements, facial nerve monitoring improves outcomes in some skull base and temporal bone surgeries.
The same statements also stress that monitoring does not replace good surgical technique.
The recording made from the start to the end of the operation is also a record of the process.

ogeler.metin: When the facial nerve is at risk

cumleler: The best-known use of monitoring is surgery for tumors of the cerebellopontine angle and internal auditory canal.
In these operations the facial nerve is almost always monitored; if hearing is to be preserved, the auditory pathway is monitored too.
Microvascular decompression, in which a blood vessel pressing on cranial nerves is moved away, is another example.
In some middle ear and mastoid operations, facial nerve monitoring may be used if the course of the nerve is at risk.
For hearing monitoring to be meaningful, there must be usable hearing and a recordable auditory brainstem response before surgery.
This prerequisite makes the preoperative audiological assessment part of the monitoring plan.

ogeler.metin: From the scalp, at a distance

cumleler: In operations that aim to preserve hearing, the auditory pathway can be monitored in three different ways.
The most common is the auditory brainstem response, or ABR, recorded with electrodes placed on the scalp.
Because the ABR is small, many sweeps must be averaged; a new result can sometimes take minutes.

cumleler.yazi: In electrocochleography, or ECochG, a fine needle is passed through the eardrum and placed on the promontory.
cumleler.ses: In electrocochleography, or E cock G, a fine needle is passed through the eardrum and placed on the promontory.

cumleler: Being close to the cochlea, the response is large and obtained much faster, but it shows only the cochlea and the distal nerve.
In the third method, the surgeon places a small electrode on the auditory nerve near the brainstem and records its response directly.
This direct recording gives a large, fast response, but the electrode must not shift.
Before surgery starts, after anesthesia is given, a baseline recording is made; all comparisons are made against it.
The dashed line shows the baseline recording, and the solid line a recording made during surgery.
In this example wave five is delayed while wave one stays in place, so the wave one to five interval has lengthened.
Many centers treat a wave five latency increase of about one millisecond, or an amplitude drop of about half, as a warning.
However, warning criteria vary from center to center, and the speed of the change also matters.
Complete loss of wave five suggests a high risk of losing hearing.

sahneler.baslik: Not every change comes from the *nerve*
cumleler: Not every change in the ABR means nerve damage; technical causes are ruled out first.
An insert earphone shifting in the ear canal, or fluid filling the canal, can reduce the stimulus.
Noise and electrical artifact from the bone drill and electrosurgical instruments disrupt the recording.
A drop in body temperature and large changes in blood pressure can also prolong latencies.

cumleler.yazi: A problem in the labyrinthine artery disrupts the blood supply to the cochlea; in that case the ECochG response may also disappear quickly.
cumleler.ses: A problem in the labyrinthine artery disrupts the blood supply to the cochlea; in that case the E cock G response may also disappear quickly.

cumleler: Making this distinction is one of the most important tasks of the person doing the monitoring.

cumleler.yazi: The facial nerve is monitored with fine needle electrodes placed in the facial muscles; this is called electromyography, or EMG.
cumleler.ses: The facial nerve is monitored with fine needle electrodes placed in the facial muscles; this is called electromyography, or E M G.

cumleler: The electrodes are usually placed in the orbicularis oculi, around the eye, and the orbicularis oris, around the mouth.
When the nerve is touched or gently pulled, a short single discharge appears in the muscle; this is often harmless.
Longer groups of short discharges, or bursts, show that the nerve has been stressed for a while.
Regular trains of discharges lasting for seconds suggest the nerve is under serious stress.
In particular, the total duration of sinusoidal trains called A-trains is linked to the risk of facial palsy after surgery.

cumleler.yazi: The EMG signal is also sent to a loudspeaker, so the surgeon hears discharges instantly without looking at the screen.
cumleler.ses: The E M G signal is also sent to a loudspeaker, so the surgeon hears discharges instantly without looking at the screen.

cumleler.yazi: Free-running EMG is monitored continuously throughout surgery and shows mechanical or heat-related stress on the nerve.
cumleler.ses: Free-running E M G is monitored continuously throughout surgery and shows mechanical or heat-related stress on the nerve.

cumleler.yazi: In triggered EMG, the surgeon stimulates tissue with a probe that delivers a small electric current.
cumleler.ses: In triggered E M G, the surgeon stimulates tissue with a probe that delivers a small electric current.

cumleler: If the facial nerve is at the stimulated spot, the facial muscles respond, which locates the nerve on the tumor.
This is especially valuable in large tumors, where the nerve is thinned and hard to see.
After the tumor is removed, the end of the nerve near the brainstem is stimulated at low current.
A clear response at low current is a positive sign that facial nerve function after surgery will be good.
Muscle relaxants block the muscle response to nerve stimulation, so with facial nerve monitoring their use is planned with anesthesia.
This planning is discussed before surgery, because the choice of drugs is entirely the anesthesia team's decision.
The ABR is relatively little affected by general anesthetic drugs, so it is a reliable monitoring tool in the operating room.
The middle latency and cortical responses we saw in earlier lessons, however, are markedly suppressed under anesthesia.
Body temperature, blood pressure and drug changes are entered in the recording notes, making it easier to understand the cause of a change.
Before surgery, the person's audiogram, ABR and facial nerve function are reviewed; without an ABR, hearing monitoring cannot be planned.
After anesthesia, the electrodes are placed, the insert earphone is secured in the canal and impedances are checked.

cumleler.yazi: Before surgery begins, baseline recordings are made for the ABR and EMG.
cumleler.ses: Before surgery begins, baseline recordings are made for the ABR and E M G.

cumleler: Recordings are watched continuously; when a meaningful change occurs, the surgeon is told at once, in clear and brief words.
The time of each warning, what the surgeon was doing at that moment and what happened next are noted.
At the end of surgery, final recordings are made and the whole process is documented in a report.
In the operating room, the surgeon, the anesthesia team and the monitoring specialist work as a team.
The anesthesia team manages drugs and vital signs and provides suitable conditions for monitoring.
The person doing the monitoring makes the recordings, recognizes artifact, and interprets and reports meaningful changes.
The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association, or ASHA, sees this as in scope for audiologists with the right knowledge and skills.
However, operating room monitoring requires additional training and supervised experience beyond basic audiology education.
The professions doing this work and the legal regulations differ from country to country.
A purely illustrative case: during tumor removal, wave five latency increases by about one millisecond over several successive recordings.
The earphone is in place, electrode impedances have not changed, and there is no new noise source in the room.
The finding is reported to the surgeon with the time; the surgeon reduces traction on the nerve and waits a few minutes.
Meanwhile, recordings are repeated at short intervals.
Within a few minutes, wave five returns close to its baseline value, and the operation continues.
The whole process is entered in the report with time stamps; the values are for teaching purposes.

sahneler.metin: Before warning, quickly rule out a technical cause: earphone, electrodes, noise. Report a real change without delay, in one clear sentence.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: in the operating room, both false alarms and late warnings undermine trust.
When you see a change, first quickly check the earphone, the electrode impedances and the noise in the room.
If there is no technical cause, do not wait; tell the surgeon what changed, by how much and since when, in one short, clear sentence.
Agreeing on this way of communicating with the surgeon before the operation makes your job easier in a crisis.

maddeler.metin: Hearing: ABR, ECochG, direct nerve recording
Facial nerve: free-running and triggered EMG

cumleler: Intraoperative monitoring aims to catch a change in nerve function before permanent damage occurs.

cumleler.yazi: Hearing is monitored with the ABR, ECochG or direct recording from the auditory nerve; changes are judged against the baseline.
cumleler.ses: Hearing is monitored with the ABR, E cock G or direct recording from the auditory nerve; changes are judged against the baseline.

cumleler.yazi: The facial nerve is monitored from the facial muscles with free-running and triggered EMG; long trains suggest serious stress.
cumleler.ses: The facial nerve is monitored from the facial muscles with free-running and triggered E M G; long trains suggest serious stress.

cumleler.yazi: Muscle relaxants block the EMG; successful monitoring needs constant communication with the anesthesia team and the surgeon.
cumleler.ses: Muscle relaxants block the E M G; successful monitoring needs constant communication with the anesthesia team and the surgeon.

sahneler.soru: When monitoring facial nerve EMG, which causes a recording problem?
sahneler.aciklama: Muscle relaxants block the muscle's response to nerve stimulation, so no discharges appear in the EMG.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: when monitoring facial nerve EMG, which of the following can block the recording?
cumleler.ses: Test yourself: when monitoring facial nerve E M G, which of the following can block the recording?

cumleler: The correct answer is A: a muscle relaxant drug.
Muscle relaxants block the muscle's response to signals from the nerve, so their use is planned in advance with the anesthesia team.
